module

public import Mathlib.Data.Set.Card

@[expose] public section

/-!
# Sunflowers

This file defines sunflowers of set families.
-/

variable {α : Type*}

/--
A sunflower `F` with kernel `S` is a collection of sets in which all possible distinct pairs of sets
share the same intersection `S`.
-/
def IsSunflowerWithKernel (F : Set (Set α)) (S : Set α) : Prop :=
  F.Pairwise (fun A B => A ∩ B = S)

theorem isSunflowerWithKernel_empty (S : Set α) : IsSunflowerWithKernel {} S := by
  simp [IsSunflowerWithKernel]

theorem isSunflowerWithKernel_singleton (S : Set α) (A : Set α) :
    IsSunflowerWithKernel {A} S := by
  simp [IsSunflowerWithKernel]

/--
A sunflower `F` is a collection of sets in which all possible distinct pairs of sets share the
same intersection.
-/
def IsSunflower (F : Set (Set α)) : Prop := ∃ S, IsSunflowerWithKernel F S

theorem isSunflower_empty : IsSunflower (∅ : Set (Set α)) := by
  simp [IsSunflower, isSunflowerWithKernel_empty]

theorem isSunflower_singleton (A : Set α) : IsSunflower {A} := by
  simp [IsSunflower, isSunflowerWithKernel_singleton]

findings.description: The pure pairwise condition at lines 34–35 leaves a singleton family's kernel completely unconstrained, as the lemma at lines 40–42 explicitly confirms. For example, `IsSunflowerWithKernel {({0} : Set ℕ)} {1}` holds even though `{1} ⊆ {0}` is false. This is weaker than the standard common-core meaning of a kernel. I classify this as a modelling-choice warning because the file deliberately documents the pairwise convention. It does not change the unparameterized `IsSunflower` predicate or either current problem use site.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Rado, “Intersection theorems for systems of sets” (1960), p. 85, explicitly stipulates `K ⊂ X_{μ₀}` for a one-member system; the footnote defines this symbol as inclusion in the wide sense. Arbitrary kernels are allowed for the empty system. See https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1960-04.pdf. Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang, “Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma,” Definition 1.1, uses the stronger canonical convention `K = S₁ ∩ ⋯ ∩ Sᵣ` (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1908.08483). Neither convention permits a singleton kernel outside its sole member.
findings.suggested_fix: To follow the original common-kernel convention, conjoin `(∀ A ∈ F, S ⊆ A)` with the current pairwise condition. Replace the arbitrary-kernel singleton lemma with one assuming `S ⊆ A`, or an iff characterizing that containment. The empty-family lemma remains valid. The containment condition is automatic for families with two distinct members, and adding it leaves `IsSunflower` equivalent to its current definition; both facts were proved in `/workspace/review/kernel_boundary.lean`.

reformulations.difference: Lean existentially quantifies a pairwise kernel instead of requiring every distinct pair's intersection to equal the intersection of the whole family, as in Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang's definition.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a family with at least two distinct members, a common pairwise intersection necessarily equals `⋂₀ F`: every element of a pairwise intersection belongs to every other member. For empty and singleton families, both pairwise conditions are vacuous. Thus, for every F, `IsSunflower F ↔ F.Pairwise (fun A B => A ∩ B = ⋂₀ F)`. I also proved equivalence to pairwise disjointness of the petals `A \ ⋂₀ F`, and to the existence of a pairwise kernel contained in every member. Consequently the singleton-kernel convention flagged above does not alter this predicate.

reformulations.difference: The source asks for positive constants c_k; Lean uses one function `c : ℕ → ℕ` and does not separately assert positivity.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For positive n, natural-number bases and positive-real bases give equivalent bounds. A positive real base can be rounded up to its natural ceiling, preserving the bound by monotonicity of powers. Conversely, cast a natural base to ℝ; the n = 1 inequality forces that base to be positive. Choosing the bases simultaneously is ordinary choice. The exact iff, instantiated with `Erdos20.f`, was proved in `/workspace/review/constants.lean`.

review.notes: Checked all six declarations and both direct problem use sites. No duplicate sunflower/delta-system definition was found in Mathlib. For Erdős 20, positive uniformity and positive thresholds force the relevant sets and families to be finite; for Erdős 857, the Fin n universe guarantees finiteness and a nonempty threshold set. Boundary threshold identities were proved. Four scratch files compile without errors or warnings. Computational tests, linked by proved equivalences to the actual predicates, cover empty types/families, singletons, pairs, disjoint and nonempty-core sunflowers, and rejection of the three two-element subsets of a three-element set. All 256 families on a three-element universe were enumerated. No repository files were edited.
